newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end mostly down after morning zigzag.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end mostly down after morning zigzag.

text.p: U.S. stocks ended mostly weaker as Friday the 13th wrought havoc on an already vulnerable Wall Street, sending the Dow industrials through a series of erratic morning gyrations.

"The final analysis is -- it's been a rocky week," said Larry Wachtel, a market analyst at Prudential Securities. "We have triple witching next Friday (and Tuesday's FOMC meeting), so there'll be lots more thrills and chills before this episode is over."
The Dow industrials rose one to about 6304.

It was another turbulent session that saw the Dow skid 50 points to trigger NYSE curbs at 1005 EST/1505 GMT, halve losses to have the curbs lifted seven minutes later and then surge more than 40 points before midday. Afternoon dealings were relatively calm, a marked contrast from the past two sessions, which shaved 170 points off the Dow.
For the week, the blue chip index lost about 77 points for the week.
Other key stock indices ended lower Friday. The Nasdaq Composite shed 13 to about 1285 as Intel and Oracle notched losses. The S&P 500 lost one to about 728.
Losers beat gainers 7-5 on very heavy NYSE volume of 454 million. The long bond rose 22/32 to yield 6.57 percent.

"Bonds are back up, which definitely helped the market. This morning we had extreme volatility and that's been the case for eight or nine sessions now. That's likely to continue to be the case going into early 1997," Ricky Harrington of Interstate/Johnson Lane said.

"We have been through a period ... where market volatility has been below average, so the type of change in the last couple of weeks is a change in character. When there's a change in character, there may be a change in trend," he said.

The Dow briefly dipped in the afternoon after President Clinton sought to allay fears that a stock market slump would hurt the U.S. economy. But several analysts played down the significance of a politician's comments on the stock market.

"I think Greenspan has decided jawboning is better than using monetary policy. It looks like Clinton has decided to pick up on that," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist of Legg Mason Wood Walker. "I don't think Clinton has the same credibility. People will view it as a political statement."
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments about "irrational exuberance" in the markets sent stocks reeling last Friday.
Alan Ackerman, a market strategist at Fahnestock and Co, was one person who was happy the week was over. "The market was vulnerable and volatile. It kept a lot of traders off-balance."
Technology stocks were broadly lower because of "Oracle and the tired blood of Intel," Prudential's Wachtel said.
After recent strong gains, Intel lost 4-1/2 to 132-3/8.

Oracle lost 3-1/4 to 44 after reporting second-quarter earnings rose to $0.27 a share from $0.20. That was a penny less than Wall Street's consensus estimate, according to Zack's Investment Research. Cowen downgraded the stock.
Micron lost one to 35-1/2, Iomega shed 1-1/4 to 18-3/4 and Microsoft fell one to 80. But IBM added 3/4 to 152-3/8.

Among individual issues, Federal Express rose 1-1/2 to 41-5/8. FedEx reported higher second-quarter earnings. It also announced a temporary two percent surcharge to all express package shipments, citing "stubbornly high" fuel prices.
Quaker Oats added two to 37-1/8 amid renewed speculation it may shed its Snapple and Gatorade businesses. Quaker declined comment on market rumors.
Forcenergy added 4-1/8 to 34-1/4. Lehman started coverage of the stock with outperform.
Zoltek lost 3-1/2 to 40 after a Merrill downgrade.

American Express fell 1/8 to 53-3/4, and Citicorp added 5/8 to 99-1/4. The Wall Street Journal reported Citicorp held unsuccessful talks to acquire AmEx. Citicorp declined comment, and AmEx said it was not engaged in talks with anyone regarding a sale of the company or any part of it.

Philip Morris lost 2-3/8 to 111-1/2 its first day of trading after going ex-dividend. A Florida judge ruled that a lawsuit against the tobacco industry, which includes claims under the state's anti-racketeering laws, would go to trial next June.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 13.42 to 1284.91.
The S&P 500 fell 0.66 to 728.64.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT).
-- Wall Street Desk 212-859-1721
